stories.headline: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO, and the stock jumps 31% in a day
stories.why_read: The AI economy's most important chip company just reversed its own leadership decision in weeks. That ripples into GPU supply, prices and every inference roadmap.
body: Nvidia's board said Monday it voted unanimously to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO, effective immediately, after "a series of discussions and meetings" with him. The board said it had "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and was confident his return "poses no national security risk." Huang resigned earlier this month after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman The New York Times says was in contact with a Chinese Ministry of State Security officer. Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, stays on as CFO.

The market's verdict was loud: per CNBC, shares closed up 31% after the news, having lost nearly 33% since Huang admitted to an affair on Nov. 8. President Trump told CNBC Huang "did nothing wrong," and Elon Musk, Gavin Baker and Brad Gerstner had all lobbied publicly for his return. Huang said he takes the job back "with the greatest humility and renewed commitment." For weeks after his exit, the board had maintained it was not considering bringing him back.

stories.headline: Musk tells SpaceX's AI team it can't compete on models, so sell the compute
stories.why_read: A rare look inside SpaceX's AI unit: renting GPUs to Anthropic and Google is outearning Grok, and Musk says revenue per GPU is the only scoreboard that matters.
body: The New York Times reported Monday that Musk told engineers in SpaceX's AI unit the company is falling behind rivals, making it more lucrative to rent out its computing capacity than to use it for its own products. In August he renamed an internal group chat with hundreds of engineers "Sell compute because we can't compete," and he asks some of them weekly to justify their GPU use. "At the end of the day, the only thing that matters for competitiveness is revenue per GPU, not benchmarks," he wrote, per the Times as relayed by Investing.com.

The numbers behind it: the Times reported Anthropic pays about $3.1 billion a month for capacity (a rate tied to full delivery of contracted capacity, per other relays) and Google roughly $800 million, with deals that could run through 2029. SpaceX's AI segment brought in more than half its revenue last quarter, per its 10-Q. Musk's response on X: "NYT is posting the obvious as 'news'."

stories.headline: TSMC eyes a $22.6B leading-edge fab on 3,200 acres near College Station
stories.why_read: Texas could land a 2nm-class TSMC fab in Brazos County, right as Terafab rises in neighboring Grimes County.
body: Brazos County officials confirmed Monday that TSMC filed an application with the State Comptroller proposing at least one fab on just over 3,200 acres in the south of the county. KBTX reports the plant would build leading-edge logic chips on 2nm-or-better processes for AI, high-performance computing and mobile, with an estimated $22.6 billion investment and up to 2,099 direct jobs averaging $133,000 a year. The parcels are under contract but not purchased, and TSMC's filing says its agreements are not yet binding.

TSMC has applied for the state's JETI tax-incentive program, which College Station ISD would have to approve, possibly as early as mid-December. The county is weighing a break similar to the one Grimes County gave Terafab, whose construction footage Anand reposted overnight with Intel's and TSMC's largest fabs overlaid for scale.

stories.headline: OpenAI and Cisco open-source Shirudo, eBPF shields that agents can write against live exploits
stories.why_read: Agents that patch the gap between disclosure and deploy, using eBPF on running Linux boxes. This is the infra-security pattern to watch.
body: Shirudo (Japanese for "shield") is an open-source Linux runtime that lets operators test and deploy temporary eBPF "shields" that block the code path a vulnerability exposes while letting legitimate requests through, so a service can keep running while the real patch is tested. In OpenAI's controlled demo, a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without a restart.

The design leans on guardrails an ops team will recognize: shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading, pass the kernel's eBPF verifier, can run in monitor mode before enforcing, and a TPM keeps a verifiable record of what was loaded or removed. Agents can investigate, draft and validate shields, but humans approve what ships. A walkthrough from Linux Plumbers Conference is linked from the post.

stories.headline: Stalwart 1.2 becomes an open-source drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange
stories.why_read: Outlook clients can now talk to an AGPL mail server via MAPI, EWS and ActiveSync. That is a real exit ramp from on-prem Exchange.
body: Stalwart 1.2.0 implements the protocols Exchange clients speak: MAPI over HTTP, Exchange Web Services, Exchange ActiveSync and Autodiscover. Outlook, Apple Mail and phone mail apps connect as if to an Exchange server, with mail, calendars, contacts, tasks and notes in one account, and the support ships in the open-source Community edition under the AGPL.

The post argues the timing is right: Exchange 2016 and 2019 left support in October 2025, Subscription Edition is the last on-prem version, and Microsoft's new Outlook for Windows doesn't support on-prem Exchange accounts. Stalwart is already in production elsewhere: Kagi says its new Kagi Mail, $99 a year after a 60-day free trial, runs on the Stalwart server with IMAP, JMAP and CalDAV. Kagi Mail is now in public beta.

stories.headline: Ladybird, the from-scratch browser engine, ships its first alpha for macOS and Linux
stories.why_read: The first new independent browser engine in years that you can download, not just compile. The 2,000-point HN thread says people want it.
body: The Ladybird team says it is now in alpha: a browser built on its own engine "from the ground up, and not a fork," with a modest but functional UI around it. Builds are available for macOS and Linux on a rolling channel with regular automatic updates, so you no longer have to build from source to follow progress.

It's honest about the state: some sites won't work, it will crash, and there are "no promises about security today"; the team explicitly invites security researchers to break it. Web developers can test with WebDriver and the Firefox DevTools protocol, and broken sites can be reported from inside the browser.

stories.headline: NariQ squeezes Qwen3.8-27B into 10 GB and matches BF16 on agentic coding
stories.why_read: A 27B open model that runs on a single GPU and holds up on long-horizon agent tasks. That's the local-inference story in one table.
body: Nari Labs released NariQ GGUFs of Qwen3.8-27B at 3, 2.5 and 2 bits per weight. NariQ is a trellis-coded post-training quantization calibrated on real coding-agent traces. On its model card the 3-bit file (10.1 GB, versus 53.8 GB for BF16) scores 41.0% on DeepSWE and 63.8% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, against 39.8% and 62.6% for BF16. The 2-bit file falls off noticeably.

The evaluation detail is the part worth reading: agent runs drove the local model through the Claude Code CLI with a 262K context, averaged over three rounds, and the card compares against Unsloth's published dynamic quants. One catch: you need Nari's llama.cpp fork to run them.

stories.headline: Virginia and Oregon sue SpaceX and X over Grok's sexualized deepfakes
stories.why_read: State consumer-protection law aimed squarely at an AI image tool's design choices, not just its users.
body: Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield filed separate but coordinated suits Monday against SpaceX Super Intelligence (formerly xAI), X Corp. and SpaceX. They allege Grok's image tools produced non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material while the companies claimed adequate safeguards. Oregon's complaint says the defendants marketed a "spicy mode" and stripped out industry-standard protections; Virginia's invokes its Consumer Protection Act.

Both states seek injunctions, disgorgement and civil penalties. These are allegations; no court has ruled. NPR reports X says it keeps updating its safeguards to keep up with new tactics from people who violate its terms.

stories.headline: An on-chain autopsy of a suspiciously timed Polymarket bet on Huang's return
stories.why_read: Prediction markets keep leaking news early. This piece follows one wallet's trades minute by minute.
body: A French-language investigation on HN's front page traces bets on Polymarket's "Will Jensen Huang rejoin NVIDIA by December 31, 2026?" market. The author says their monitoring algorithm flagged a wallet that swept the order book at about 6.5% odds, finishing its buys 89 minutes before Trump posted about Huang on Truth Social, and turned 4,648 USDC into 71,518 USDC.

The wallet was a fresh Gnosis Safe proxy created 81 hours earlier, with no other activity. The author argues chance is statistically ruled out. That remains their analysis, not a finding by any regulator, but it pairs with a separate HN post tracking which Washington officials hold Nvidia stock.

stories.headline: LeCun: Amodei hypes AI dangers so open models get outlawed
stories.why_read: The open-versus-closed fight just got personal, with 1,700 points and 1,000 HN comments.
body: Replying to a clip of Dario Amodei's congressional testimony on open-source AI, Yann LeCun wrote that "Dario's spiel since GPT-2 has always been about hyping the dangers so that open models would be made illegal and *he* would stay in control," and compared it to the Ottoman Empire restricting the printing press to keep control of dogma. "It's a new form of medieval obscurantism," he added.

Whatever you think of the jab, the debate underneath is live policy: whether frontier weights should ship at all, and who gets to hold the off switch. Amodei's argument, as the clip summarizes it, is that closed models can be monitored and cut off while released weights can never be recalled.

stories.headline: Claude Code's experimental Code Mode lets the agent script its own tool calls
stories.why_read: Fewer round-trips, less context bloat, and background jobs for up to two hours. Harness design is where the coding-agent gains are now.
body: Opt in with CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 and Claude writes JavaScript that chains tools like Bash, Read and Edit, running steps in parallel and filtering output before it hits the context window, instead of calling one tool at a time. Addy Osmani says it shines for multi-file audits, batch edits and parallel search-and-filter jobs, and you can expand the generated code with Ctrl+O.

In auto or bypassPermissions mode, scripts can run in the background for up to two hours while you keep working, managed with /tasks. Every generated tool call still goes through your deny and ask rules, sandbox limits and PreToolUse hooks, and hooks can inspect the script before it runs.

stories.headline: Anthropic folds connectors and skills into plugins, and redesigns Claude Code's desktop panel
stories.why_read: Two Claude updates Anand reposted overnight: one install path for tools and skills, and tabs for files, diffs and terminal.
body: Claude now treats connectors and skills as a single thing: plugins, which can connect a tool, teach a skill or do both. They're live on Free, Pro, Max and Ultra plans, with Team and Enterprise coming soon, and Anthropic says there are 10,000+ to browse.

Separately, Claude Code on desktop got a redesigned side panel: Files, Changes, Terminal and other tools open as tabs beside your session, and you can split them or pop one into its own window. It's rolling out on Mac first, with Windows and Linux coming soon.

stories.headline: Google passes OpenAI in OpenRouter spend, and Gemini 4 Neon is why
stories.why_read: Where developers actually spend money is a better benchmark than any leaderboard, and last week it tilted to Google.
body: OpenRouter says its users spent more money on Google models than OpenAI models last week, crediting "multiple well-received launches, including Gemini 4 Neon and Carbon" for pushing Google past the 50% mark.

The anecdotes match: DHH says Neon cut Omarchy's boot time in half and made big install optimizations, describing it as "a quiet cat" that works with little output and then delivers everything at once.

stories.headline: Rebuttal: OpenAI's perplexity-drop chart may mostly measure more code in training
stories.why_read: Yesterday's OpenAI 'perplexity as intelligence' chart gets a sharp, sourced pushback on what the corpus actually was.
body: micjm points out that OpenAI's chart of falling perplexity across model generations is, per a footnote, measured on a fixed corpus of code. That raises an obvious confound: newer models may simply be trained on more code. They cite a paper that trained a 160M model on five data mixes varying only the code share; the 75%-code variant shows the same kind of perplexity drop on code while getting dramatically worse on non-code text.

The author's point isn't that the chart measures nothing, just that it needs far more qualifications. They also note OpenAI itself footnotes that code prediction is "a poor proxy" for general capability in GPT-2 and GPT-3.

stories.headline: Qwen 32B can tell when a concept was injected into its context, even while denying it
stories.why_read: A crisp interpretability result: the model notices the tampering internally even when it says otherwise.
body: The paper finds a Qwen 32B model can detect when concepts were injected into earlier context and identify which one, even though its sampled outputs deny any injection. Logit-lens analysis shows clear detection signals in the residual stream that fade in the final layers.

Telling the model accurately how AI introspection works boosts sensitivity from 0.3% to 39.9% with only a 0.6% rise in false positives, and mutual information between injected and recovered concepts rises from 0.61 to 1.05 bits. The authors flag consequences for latent reasoning and safety.

stories.headline: Harmonic's Aristotle proves a Celeste Classic speedrun can never be beaten
stories.why_read: Lean-checked optimality for a real game, and a fun showcase of how AI provers prune impossible search spaces.
body: Aristotle translated the PICO-8 platformer Celeste Classic into Lean, then proved that the computer-assisted 2,843-frame run is optimal across all possible input sequences. In a separate category it set a new record and proved that time optimal too.

Brute force is hopeless (36 inputs per frame, rooms up to 172 frames), so the proof stacks tricks: a "climb bound" of 3 pixels per frame, merged subpixel states, dominance pruning and per-room tables. In the hardest room it checked only about 224 million states.

stories.headline: Cheaper tokens won't pay for $560B of hyperscaler capex, one analyst argues
stories.why_read: Clear arithmetic on whether Jevons' paradox actually rescues AI spending. It sets up the bank-loan story below.
body: Philipp Dubach's core point: revenue is price times volume, and token volumes and token prices are moving at roughly the same speed. Google went from 9.7 trillion tokens a month in May 2024 to 3.2 quadrillion in May 2026, but research finds the price of fixed capability falling 5-13x a year. Economists estimating elasticities from OpenRouter and Azure data found them "just above one," leaving "limited scope for Jevons-Paradox effects."

Meanwhile five hyperscalers spent $560 billion on capex in the first three quarters of 2026. His conclusion: closing the gap needs money that today pays for labor, which is why vendors are reaching for outcome pricing.

stories.headline: Banks start offloading AI data-center loans at a discount
stories.why_read: If lenders flinch, the data-center buildout slows regardless of demand. This is the credit side of the AI trade.
body: Per posts summarized by X News, HSBC reportedly sold $300 million of data-center loans at roughly 85 cents on the dollar, while ING struggled to offload $500 million and is negotiating individual sales. Regulators are paying attention: the ECB is weighing a review of about €200 billion in AI lending, and the Bank of England is questioning banks about speculative data-center loans.

Martin Pelletier notes that Goldman expects hyperscaler debt issuance to jump from $250 billion in 2026 to $420 billion in 2027, just as lenders turn cautious, and compares the setup to the shale boom.

stories.headline: AMD EPYC Zen 6 versus Zen 1: 12.1x faster in under a decade, up to 133x in AI
stories.why_read: A clean decade-long benchmark on the same software stack. Useful perspective for anyone sizing a refresh.
body: Phoronix pulled AMD's original 2017 Naples review server (dual EPYC 7601: 32 cores, 180W each) out of storage and ran it against the new EPYC 9006 "Venice" parts: the 256-core EPYC 9996, with 1 GB of L3 and 16 channels of MRDIMM-12800, and the frequency-optimized 9686F. Both new chips are rated at 600W.

Across real-world workloads on Ubuntu 26.10, the geometric-mean speedup was 12.1x, peaking at 133x in AI workloads. The review also tracks power efficiency, which matters more than raw throughput for most datacenters.

stories.headline: trynix.dev now boots GUI Linux apps, including Firefox, in your browser
stories.why_read: Linux compiled to WebAssembly, with Wayland, GL and sound. 'The Birth & Death of JavaScript' arrives nine years early.
body: Farid Zakaria's trynix.dev already ran any of 300,000+ Nix package versions in the browser via QEMU, but slowly. It has now switched to unkernel, Linux compiled to WebAssembly by Pooya Parsa and published Nov. 19, where the kernel runs at wasm speed and only user programs are emulated. He reports 2x to 32x speedups depending on workload.

It now runs graphical programs: Wayland surfaces are composited in the page, a minimal Mesa virgl build renders through WebGL2, and there's an ALSA sound card. Try solitaire, GL gears, xeyes or Firefox.

stories.headline: Arm's lawyers force down the beloved AArch64 instruction reference site
stories.why_read: A widely used, searchable ISA reference is going away on Dec. 4. Bookmark or mirror what you need now.
body: Jon's arm.jonpalmisc.com offered fast, searchable reference documentation for AArch64 instructions and system registers across Armv8-A and Armv9-A. He says Arm's lawyers told him to take it down or face legal action, so it will be discontinued on 4 December 2026.
He thanked fans "even the ones at Arm" and says he'll look for ways to keep bookmarks and links working. Its search runs in WebAssembly, and it covers both instructions and system registers.

stories.headline: Quad9 switches off DNS for all of France rather than block sites for beIN
stories.why_read: A public resolver choosing to exit a country over court-ordered blocking is a big precedent for internet plumbing.
body: As of 09:00 Paris time today, Nov. 24, Quad9 refuses every query from French users. French courts upheld demands from sports rightsholder beIN that Quad9 block domains tied to piracy streams, and Quad9 faced fines for not complying.

Quad9 says it opposes piracy but rejects being drafted into content enforcement against third parties, arguing that blocking at recursive resolvers does nothing to the origin servers. French users still pointed at 9.9.9.9 will simply lose resolution until they switch.

stories.headline: UT Austin's Arctic: a lock-free adaptive radix tree that speeds up RocksDB by up to 40%
stories.why_read: Austin systems research at OSDI: high performance, lock freedom and range scans in one index, which was supposed to be a pick-two.
body: Arctic, from UT Austin researchers including Emmett Witchel, with ETH Zürich, is a lock-free adaptive radix tree that beats lock-based indexes, including a concurrent hash map, on many YCSB configurations. It also supports range and prefix scans, which hash maps can't.

It guarantees non-blocking operation via careful metadata layout and a freezing-based coordination protocol, and adds a new safe memory-reclamation scheme. Dropped into RocksDB and Turso in place of their default skiplists, it raised write-heavy throughput by up to 40% and 12%.

stories.headline: C++26 is done, again, after contracts sent it back for a second vote
stories.why_read: First time an ISO C++ draft failed its approval ballot. The contracts fight shows how hard safety features are to standardize.
body: Herb Sutter reports that the C++26 draft, finished in March, failed to pass its international approval ballot unanimously, a first, mostly over the contracts feature (pre, post and contract_assert). At the six-day meeting in Búzios, Brazil, the committee addressed the comments, adopted an extension to contracts, and is sending an updated document out for a second ballot.

For C++29 they adopted labeled break and continue, std::ranges::any_view and views::slice. About 220 people attended, with remote participation higher than usual because of the U.S. aviation ground stop.

stories.headline: Mitchell Hashimoto explains why Rex ships a Windows client before Linux
stories.why_read: Pragmatic product sequencing from the Ghostty/HashiCorp founder, and a Rex roadmap update.
body: Mitchell Hashimoto says Rex will ship full Linux and FreeBSD server support soon, but Windows clients come before Linux ones. His reasoning: there are more developers on Windows than every other desktop OS combined, desktop Linux has a lot of ways to do things and strong opinions about each, and the team found a talented Windows developer early who is already on it full time.
He has shipped desktop Linux software almost full time for years, he says, so the team wants to get the Linux client right, or at least communicate it right. The video has the long version.

stories.headline: Product engineering versus factory engineering: building the agents that build the product
stories.why_read: A useful frame for how an architect's job is splitting, plus Armin Ronacher's case for better software, not more of it.
body: Ben Holmes argues there are now two kinds of engineering. Product engineering decides what should exist and how it's architected. Factory engineering builds the system of agents that implements and reviews it: not full automation, but automating low-risk work and asking for human attention only when necessary.

Armin Ronacher's AI Engineer talk, now online, pulls the other way on output: a year of lessons and an argument for better, not more, software. Together they sketch the same shift from writing code to designing the process that writes it.

stories.headline: Tesla stock is roughly flat over five years, despite going from FSD Beta to driverless robotaxis
stories.why_read: A blunt reality check on what the market is and isn't pricing in for autonomy.
body: Whole Mars Catalog points out that TSLA is down about 7% compared with five years ago, a span in which Tesla went from FSD Beta to driverless robotaxis. Per X's news summary, the stock has traded in a range around $360 and recently slipped near $346, even with robotaxi service running in Austin and Dallas.
Per the same summary, investors are debating whether past hype already priced in the growth or whether the market undervalues a scaling autonomous service.

stories.headline: TACC's Horizon opens: the fastest academic supercomputer in the U.S. is in Austin
stories.why_read: A 4,000-GPU NSF machine down the road from Anand, built for both AI and simulation.
body: Horizon, the centerpiece of the NSF Leadership-Class Computing Facility at UT Austin's Texas Advanced Computing Center, is open to early users. It has 4,000 GPUs and ranks No. 24 on the November 2026 TOP500 at 132 petaflops on HPL, making it the most powerful academic system in the country. With it, TACC has nearly 5,500 GPUs.

Performance will climb further when its CPU partition arrives in early 2027. Dell, NVIDIA and VAST Data are the main partners, and NSF calls it its biggest-ever investment in computing infrastructure.

stories.headline: Why a jet engine is harder to build than a nuke: single-crystal turbine blades
stories.why_read: A great short explainer on one of materials science's quiet miracles, the kind of physics-and-chemistry story Anand pins.
body: Christian Ciabattoni notes that nine countries have built nuclear weapons but only five can produce high-end jet engines, and only four of those make both commercial and fighter engines. The bottleneck is turbine blades, which face roughly 3,600°F, about 10 tons of force each, and tens of thousands of hours of service.

Ordinary castings form many small crystals whose boundaries become weak points at those temperatures. The answer, decades and billions of dollars in the making, is nickel superalloy blades cast as a single crystal.

stories.headline: WashU's hydrogel gets stronger the more you bend it
stories.why_read: Most materials fatigue. This one reorganizes under strain, like collagen, and could protect joints and tissue.
body: A team led by chemist Chenfeng Ke at Washington University in St. Louis reports in Nature Materials a 3D-printable, biodegradable hydrogel made from sugar crystals and polyethylene glycol that strengthens where it is strained. Ring-shaped cyclodextrin molecules slide into position to reinforce stressed regions as the polymers become more uniform and organized.
On a knee-like test joint it was bent 10,000 times and performed as predicted. "It can remember, adapt, learn and grow," Ke said. The team is eyeing medical uses for protecting and repairing tissue.
